final.style: ONE LIFE, EVERY STEP. The whole life of B.K.S. Iyengar (1918 to 2014), one step per slide, in time order: a sick baby, a stiff boy his teacher doubted, a strong and brave young teacher at 18, a bad fall at 60, a slow comeback, a curious mind at 86, a calm old teacher, three hours of practice a day near 90, then a gentle end at 95. The big word is in CAPS inside the small text, as in the other ladder sets.
final.title: The Sick Boy Who Climbed to 95
final.stakes: If you do nothing, the steps still come: sickness, injury, getting old. Nobody skips them. You just meet them with a body you never trained and no habit to come back to.
final.why_care: You are on one of these steps today, and the next one is already coming. Iyengar started life sick and was badly hurt at 60. Each time, he came back to his daily practice, and near 90 he still did three hours of asanas a day. What you practise this year is what you carry into your next step.

slides.text: A healthy life does not skip the hard steps. HOPE is climbing each one stronger.
slides.source: none (the owner's message in plain words, no quote or fact)
slides.photo_hint: Wide shot of the full Mysore room, students of every age practising side by side, young at the front, older at the back. Leave calm space at the top for the big word.

slides.text: The man who helped take yoga to the world began life FRAGILE. B.K.S. Iyengar was born sick in 1918. As a boy he had malaria every year, plus typhoid and TB.
slides.credit: B.K.S. Iyengar to Harsh Desai · The Tribune, 2005 (retold) · AP, 2014
slides.source: https://www.tribuneindia.com/2005/20051204/spectrum/main1.htm : "In 1918, I was affected by influenza when I was born." "I used to contract malaria every year for many years. I also developed typhoid and was diagnosed as having TB." | https://wtop.com/news/2014/08/indian-yoga-guru-bks-iyengar-dies-at-95/ (AP, 20 Aug 2014): "who helped popularize yoga around the world"; "Iyengar was a sickly child"
slides.photo_hint: A new or very young student taking a first careful Samasthiti, small and still, soft morning light.

slides.text: Even his own teacher looked at him with DOUBT. He started yoga at 15, and his body was very stiff. He kept going anyway, practising for hours.
slides.credit: B.K.S. Iyengar to Harsh Desai · The Tribune, 2005 · Open magazine, 2014 · AP, 2014 (retold)
slides.source: https://www.tribuneindia.com/2005/20051204/spectrum/main1.htm : "He taught me for a few days and saw my body was very stiff and lost interest." | https://openthemagazine.com/voices/the-iyengar-art-of-living (Madhavankutty Pillai, 21 Aug 2014): "reluctant to teach the boy because he considered him physically weak"; "He would practice like a maniac for hours." | https://wtop.com/news/2014/08/indian-yoga-guru-bks-iyengar-dies-at-95/ (AP): "When he was 15, a relative introduced him to yoga"
slides.photo_hint: A stiff teenage or beginner student in Paschimottanasana, hands far from the feet, still trying.

slides.text: The stiff boy grew strong, then BRAVE. Two years later he "could do a lot of backbends." At 18, when no other student would go to teach in Pune, he went.
slides.credit: B.K.S. Iyengar to Harsh Desai · The Tribune, 2005 · AP, 2014
slides.source: https://www.tribuneindia.com/2005/20051204/spectrum/main1.htm : "In 1936, at a demonstration in Belgaum, a surgeon called V.B. Gokhale was impressed by me as I could do a lot of backbends." "He wanted a senior student. He wrote to Guruji. But no one was willing to go; so Guruji asked me to go. I came to Pune in 1937." | https://wtop.com/news/2014/08/indian-yoga-guru-bks-iyengar-dies-at-95/ (AP): "By the time he was 18, he moved to Pune to practice yoga and to teach its techniques to others."
slides.photo_hint: A strong young student in Urdhva Dhanurasana (backbend), full of power.

slides.text: HURT comes even to the strongest body. At 60, his scooter hit a rock. "My spine was twisted." He was told he would never practise again.
slides.credit: B.K.S. Iyengar to Harsh Desai · The Tribune, 2005 · Open magazine, 2014
slides.source: https://www.tribuneindia.com/2005/20051204/spectrum/main1.htm : (asked about 'a bad accident in 1979') "I was driving a scooter and it hit the rock and fell off because of which my spine was twisted." | https://openthemagazine.com/voices/the-iyengar-art-of-living : "After a scooter accident in 1979, he was told he would never be able to practise but he taught himself all over again."
slides.photo_hint: A middle-aged student sitting still after practice, one hand on the lower back or knee, quiet and thoughtful. No pain on the face.

slides.text: Healing was PATIENT work, even for a master. He said he recovered "only very slowly." He had to learn yoga all over again, like a beginner.
slides.credit: B.K.S. Iyengar to Harsh Desai · The Tribune, 2005 · Open magazine, 2014
slides.source: https://www.tribuneindia.com/2005/20051204/spectrum/main1.htm : "Only very slowly, did I recover. I had to virtually re-learn yoga." | https://openthemagazine.com/voices/the-iyengar-art-of-living : "he taught himself all over again"
slides.photo_hint: A student in their 50s or 60s doing a simple Surya Namaskara A slowly, like a beginner again.

slides.text: A CURIOUS mind kept him learning into his 80s. He taught himself much of his yoga by watching how the body works. At 86 he published another book, Light on Life.
slides.credit: B.K.S. Iyengar to Harsh Desai · The Tribune, 2005 · Open magazine, 2014 (retold)
slides.source: https://www.tribuneindia.com/2005/20051204/spectrum/main1.htm : "From the beginning, I had the ability to observe the body and see what was happening to it and explain it."; "on the publication of his 18th book Light on Life. He turns 87 on December 14." | https://openthemagazine.com/voices/the-iyengar-art-of-living : "he was self taught to a large extent"
slides.photo_hint: An older student looking closely at their own foot or hand alignment, focused and curious.

slides.text: The wise old teacher was CALM about slow progress. He did not trust quick yoga on TV. One student, he said, took 11 years just to know the back of her knees.
slides.source: https://openthemagazine.com/voices/the-iyengar-art-of-living : "He dismissed the instant yoga of television; results took time." "He said it took 11 years of practise to just know the back of her knees, how ridiculous was it to think that you could learn anything in a few days."
slides.photo_hint: An older student in Padmasana, eyes closed, calm face.

slides.text: Staying strong late in life takes a STUBBORN habit. In his 70s he was too weak to climb stairs. Near 90, he still did three hours of asanas a day.
slides.source: https://openthemagazine.com/voices/the-iyengar-art-of-living (meeting in 2006): his words "My friend, 10 years ago I was in a death bed at this place only. My vital energy had sapped to such an extent that I could not come to class because I could not climb staircases."; "Iyengar had finished his daily practice of three hours of asanas and an hour of pranayam"; "not bad for someone just short of 90"
slides.photo_hint: A student in their 60s or 70s holding a long, steady standing asana or Sirsasana, strong and focused.

slides.step: 9 getting weak, near the end of life
slides.text: The last step asks for PEACE, not strength. Even a strong body grows weak at the end. He practised until two months before he passed away, aged 95.
slides.source: https://wtop.com/news/2014/08/indian-yoga-guru-bks-iyengar-dies-at-95/ (AP, 20 Aug 2014): "practiced yoga until two months ago"; "died Wednesday at age 95" (sentence 2 is a plain life truth, no fact or number)
slides.photo_hint: The oldest student in the room resting in final Savasana, light from the window, peaceful.

final.caption:
Born sick. Hurt at 60. Too weak for stairs in his 70s. Still practising at 95.
Nobody skips a step of life, not even B.K.S. Iyengar.
At every step, he went back to his practice.
Which step are you on right now?
#aybkk #ashtanga #ashtangabangkok #boonchutanti #iyengar

A) REUSED PERSON. B.K.S. Iyengar is in used.txt (Light on Life 2005, Light on Yoga 1966, the 'breath' line, and on claude/bots-memory: 7 Oct, 9 Oct stay-active 2 and 4, 10 Oct). C) STUBBORN (slide 9) has to mean 'never gives up' in translation: ZH 倔强 or 不服输, TH ไม่ยอมแพ้, RU упорный (not упрямый).
D) BIG WORDS SHARED WITH SET C. HOPE, CURIOUS, CALM and PEACE are also big words in 'The Ladder: Your Steps'. The rule only asks for each word once per carousel, so this is allowed. If the 3 sets post close together, you may want to swap a few. The two covers also say almost the same thing ('not even the healthy' in C, 'A healthy life does not skip the hard steps' here).

FIXES APPLIED: cover (reader's version: says the belief outright, and the big word comes in sentence 2, like set C's cover). Slide 2: 'born with flu' became 'born sick' because of the 1918 pandemic link (fact check), and the illness list reads 'plus typhoid and TB' (reader). I did not use 'then typhoid, then TB', because the source does not give that order. Slide 4: the reader's backbends proof of strength, with no rent line and 'no other student'. Slide 5: dropped 'In 1979'. Slide 6: exact part-quote, so the odd comma is gone. Slide 7: the reader's retold version, so the 'My mind is very open' quote no longer sits out of context. Slide 8: dropped the age (fact check: by his 14 Dec 1918 birthday he was 87 for most of 2006), took the reader's story frame, and kept his own words 'just to know the back of her knees'. Slide 9: 'Near 90' (Open: 'just short of 90') with three hours of asanas a day. 'Plus pranayama' is gone. Slide 10: the reader's honest weak-at-the-end version. Stakes, why_care and caption: dropped 'every comeback is slower and harder' and 'practice brought him back'. 'Come back to practice' became 'he went back to his practice', so it does not read like a 'come practise' call.

FIXES REJECTED: the reader's slide 3 named Pattabhi Jois and used the line 'go on practising what is taught to you'. That line is Krishnamacharya's words, and he is a used person. Slide 3 now uses Open's 'practice like a maniac for hours', retold. The reader's 'At 88' (slide 8). The reader's 'headstands in his 90s' on slide 9, which repeats the posted 'I am 90 ... Sirsasana' point. I used the new Open fact instead, and the caption hook now says 'Still practising at 95' (AP).

CHECKED: on 7 Nov I downloaded the Tribune 2005, Open 2014 and AP/WTOP 2014 pages again. Every quote and retold fact was checked word for word against them, including the reader's new lines (backbends, observe the body, 11 years, staircases, just short of 90). The quotes keep the source's words, but the first letter's case changed in two: 'only very slowly' (source has 'Only') and 'My spine was twisted' (source has 'my'). Word counts: cover 15, slides 26 to 32 (slide 8 is exactly 32). Each big word is in sentence 1 (except the cover) and used once. No long dash, 'asana' only, no emoji.

OPTIONAL: Tribune 2005, exact words: 'Do you know what hatha means? It means stubborn.' This fits slide 9's idea, or a Plato Reel. It is not in the caption, to keep the caption to 2 lines plus a question. Still left out on purpose: the 1918 epidemic, the two heart attacks and the kidney illness, the 'no food' strictness, the Maharaja and the Queen of Belgium, 'poses', and numbers the sources disagree on (book count, age at death, birth date). If teacher-adjusting photos are used, keep them off back-to-back slides.

issues.problem: The set reuses a person, which the rules forbid. B.K.S. Iyengar is in used.txt: Light on Life 2005 (16 Oct be-ready), Light on Yoga 1966 (16 Oct and 17 Oct be-ready, and 'breath' in 20 Oct focus-energy). The claude/bots-memory branch shows more: 7 Oct first-time-hard (two Light on Yoga slides), 9 Oct stay-active 2 and 4, and 10 Oct myths. Two story points also repeat what was already posted. Slide 10 ('headstands in his 90s') matches the stay-active 4 slide 'I am 90 ... I stay in Sirsasana (Headstand) for half an hour'. Slides 3 and 4 match be-ready G, 'young Iyengar began yoga to grow strong for life's challenges'. Every quote in this set is new, and I checked each one word for word against the Tribune 2005, AP/WTOP 20 Aug 2014 and Open 21 Aug 2014 pages, but the rule bans the person too.
issues.fix: Boonchu must give an explicit OK for this exception (his request to tell one person's whole life fits Iyengar). Without that OK the set needs a subject who is not in used.txt. Do not publish on the current rule as it stands.

issues.problem: 'At 88' (both slides) clashes with his birth date. Open does say 'In 2006 ... he was 88 years old'. But the Tribune of 4 Dec 2005 says 'He turns 87 on December 14', so through 2006 he was 87 until 14 Dec 2006. He was 88 only if the meeting fell in the last 17 days of 2006. The writer's age check ('88 at the 2006 meeting') is wrong for almost all of that year.
issues.fix: Slide 9: change 'At 88 he did' to 'Near 90, he did' (Open: 'not bad for someone just short of 90'). That keeps 31 words. Slide 8: drop the age, so 'He said yoga results take time.'

issues.problem: 'to notice her knees were not straight' does not match the source. Open says 'she learnt that the back of her knees were not straight' and 'it took 11 years of practise to just know the back of her knees'.
issues.fix: 'It took one student 11 years to notice the backs of her knees were not straight.' Together with dropping 'At 88' the slide is 30 words.

issues.problem: 'who also taught Pattabhi Jois' brings in a second person who is already used (Pattabhi Jois: Yoga Mala and the Miele book in used.txt). It also sets AYBKK's own lineage root next to 'lost interest'. The writer already left out the 'no food' line out of respect for the lineage, and this clause works against that. The quote and its '...' trim are exact (Tribune: 'He taught me for a few days and saw my body was very stiff and lost interest.'). Open backs 'had doubts': 'reluctant to teach the boy because he considered him physically weak'.
issues.fix: Delete ', who also taught Pattabhi Jois' so the sentence reads 'At 15 he began yoga with Krishnamacharya.' (25 words). Drop the Wikipedia source, and add 'Open magazine, 2014' to the credit for the doubt line.

issues.problem: 'born with flu in India in 1918' points readers to the 1918 flu pandemic, a disaster with victims. The source sentence goes on: 'My mother, too, was affected as there was a global epidemic.' The other facts check out: AP gives 'who helped popularize yoga around the world' and 'sickly child', and the Tribune gives 'malaria every year for many years ... typhoid ... TB'.
issues.fix: 'B.K.S. Iyengar was born sick in India in 1918.' (29 words, and it matches 'Born sick.' in the caption).

issues.problem: 'his daily practice brought him back' (after two heart attacks) reads as a medical claim. 'every comeback is slower and harder' for people who do not practise is an unchecked general claim that plays on health fear. Neither is on a slide, but they could leak into the caption.
issues.fix: Keep both out of the slides and the caption. If you use them, write 'each time, he came back to his daily practice' and drop 'every comeback is slower and harder'.

issues.problem: The slide ends on a low point (his teacher lost interest) and gives no reason he kept going, so slide 4's 'strength' comes from nowhere. The trimmed quote 'He... saw my body' mixes 'He' (the teacher) and 'my' (Iyengar), which loses a 10-year-old. 'had doubts' is also not the exact big word. The Tribune interview has the turn this slide needs, word for word in the same answer: 'He said you go on practising what is taught to you.'
issues.fix: Even his teacher looked at the stiff boy with DOUBT. At 15 he began with Krishnamacharya, Pattabhi Jois's teacher. He told the boy to "go on practising what is taught to you." (32 words. Credit: B.K.S. Iyengar to Harsh Desai · The Tribune, 2005 (retold, quote exact) · AP, 2014)

issues.problem: 'Strength made the sick boy brave' claims a cause the slide never shows. Nothing on the slide proves he got strong, and this is the 'getting strong' step. 'Where no one else would go' makes Pune sound like a dangerous place, when the source means no other student would go. 'At 18, in 1937' puts two numbers in one line. The same Tribune passage has the proof of strength: in 1936 a surgeon was impressed 'as I could do a lot of backbends', two years after the stiff start. That is the owner's message in one line: practice turned a stiff boy strong.
issues.fix: The stiff boy grew strong, then BRAVE. Two years later he "could do a lot of backbends." At 18, when no other student would go to teach in Pune, he went. (31 words. The rent line can move to the caption if wanted. The photo hint, Urdhva Dhanurasana, now matches the text.)

issues.problem: The quote 'My mind is very open' is taken out of its context. In the Tribune it answers 'How did you master the art of yoga?' and is about how he learned from the beginning, not about his mind in his 80s. 'Largely self-taught' and 'brought out' are not 10-year-old words. Sentence 2 is also a fact about his whole life, dropped into the 80s step.
issues.fix: A CURIOUS mind kept him learning into his 80s. He taught himself much of his yoga by watching how the body works. At 86 he published another book, Light on Life. (31 words. Retold from Tribune 'I had the ability to observe the body and see what was happening to it' and Open 'self taught to a large extent'. No quote marks.)

issues.problem: Sentence 1 ('Calm comes when you stop chasing fast results') is preachy and switches to lecturing 'you' in a set that tells one man's story. The knee story is garbled: 'took 11 years to notice her knees were not straight' sounds like 11 years of failure. His real point was that 11 years of practice were needed just to know the back of her knees, so nobody learns yoga in a few days.
issues.fix: At 88 he was CALM about slow progress. He did not trust quick yoga on TV. One student took 11 years just to feel the back of her knees, he said. (31 words, credit Pillai · Open magazine, 2014 (retold))

issues.problem: The timeline jumps backwards. Slide 8 is at 88, then this slide goes back to his 70s and then to 88 again, so three slides in a row (86, 88, 88) feel stuck rather than climbing. 'Plus pranayama' means nothing to the 10-year-old or the office worker. Also, STUBBORN sounds like a flaw in translation (Chinese 固执, Thai ดื้อ). It needs the positive sense.
issues.fix: Staying strong late in life takes a STUBBORN habit. In his 70s he was too weak to climb stairs. He kept practising, and did headstands in his 90s. (28 words, moving the AP 'headstands in his 90s' fact here from slide 10. Translator note: use 倔强 / ไม่ยอมแพ้, the never-give-up sense. Optional: put his exact Tribune line 'Do you know what hatha means? It means stubborn' in the caption.)

issues.problem: The last step is 'getting weak, near the end', but the slide shows only strength (headstands in his 90s) and then death. Without meaning to, that promises too much: practise and you never have a weak step. 'Peace is letting go after a full climb' is a bit abstract, and 'letting go' can read as giving up. 'Aged 95, in 2014' is two numbers.
issues.fix: The last step asks for PEACE, not strength. Even a strong body grows weak at the end. He practised until two months before he passed away, aged 95. (28 words. Honest about weakness, gentle, no medical detail, and it calls back to slide 5's 'even the strongest body'. Credit: Associated Press · obituary, Aug 2014 (retold).)

issues.problem: The exact quote 'Only very slowly, did I recover' has an odd comma that looks like AYBKK's typo on a slide. The sentence 1 idea is good: an honest comeback, slow even for a master.
issues.fix: Healing was PATIENT work, even for a master. He recovered "only very slowly," he said. He had to learn yoga all over again, like a beginner. (26 words. The quoted part is an exact substring, and the comma problem is gone.)

issues.problem: 'Then came malaria every year, typhoid and TB' reads as if typhoid also came every year, and the list is choppy. 'In India in 1918' can drop 'in India' to stay under 32 words with a clearer list. FRAGILE describes a state more than a feeling, but it fits a newborn and it passes. Keep it.
issues.fix: The man who helped take yoga to the world began life FRAGILE. B.K.S. Iyengar was born with flu in 1918. As a boy he had malaria every year, then typhoid, then TB. (32 words)

issues.problem: This is the strongest slide: honest, clear, no fear, no promise. The only problem is two numbers in one line ('In 1979, at 60'), which is hard for the 10-year-old. Every other slide should also use one number at most, and give an age rather than a year.
issues.fix: Hurt comes even to the strongest body. At 60, his scooter hit a rock. "My spine was twisted." He was told he would never practise again. (26 words)

issues.problem: The cover works, but the belief it flips is only implied. The reader's real belief is 'if I live healthy I will avoid the hard steps'. Saying that belief outright makes the flip land in one second and states the owner's honest promise. Optional.
issues.fix: A healthy life does not skip the hard steps. HOPE is climbing each one stronger. (15 words. Credit unchanged.)

issues.problem: Reader-level reuse: AYBKK followers already saw Iyengar in October posts, including his 'I am 90 ... Sirsasana half an hour' quote. The headstands-in-his-90s fact repeats that point. used.txt bans any person already used, so Boonchu must decide whether Iyengar can carry this set, as the writer flagged. Otherwise the ladder reads as one real climb, honest, with a calm end and no 'every step easy' promise. The caption is strong and fits the habit direction ('come back to practice').
issues.fix: Keep the person only if Boonchu confirms that reusing Iyengar is OK with all-new quotes. If not, the set needs a new subject. No slide text change needed for this point.
